subject: Economics
name: Economics, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, The Australian economy and economic management
syllabus: VCE Economics Study Design (from 2023), Units 3 and 4

points.title: Relative scarcity and the PPF
points.brief: Needs and wants outrun resources, so choices carry an opportunity cost. The production possibility frontier shows those choices and the three economic questions.

points.title: Types of efficiency
points.brief: Allocative efficiency makes what people value most, productive efficiency uses the fewest resources, dynamic efficiency adapts over time, and intertemporal efficiency balances now against later.

points.title: Conditions for a competitive market
points.brief: A free, perfectly competitive market has many buyers and sellers, similar products, good information, free entry and exit, and no government interference.

points.title: Allocating resources through markets
points.brief: In a market economy, relative prices signal what is scarce and wanted, so resources flow to where they are valued most.

points.title: Competitive markets and living standards
points.brief: Strong competition pushes prices down, lifts quality and drives new ideas, so resources go where they are valued most and living standards rise.

points.title: The theory of the law of demand
points.brief: Demand falls as price rises because of the income effect, where buying power shrinks, and the substitution effect, where other goods look cheaper.

points.title: Non-price factors in demand
points.brief: Disposable income, prices of substitutes and complements, preferences, interest rates, population and consumer confidence shift the demand curve.

points.title: The theory of the law of supply
points.brief: Supply rises with price because the profit motive draws producers to make more when each unit earns more.

points.title: Non-price factors in supply
points.brief: Production costs, the number of suppliers, technology, productivity and the climate shift the supply curve.

points.title: Shifts and new equilibrium
points.brief: A shift in demand or supply changes the equilibrium price and quantity traded. Both curves can move at once.

points.title: Price elasticity of demand
points.brief: How much quantity demanded responds to a price change. Necessities, goods with few substitutes, cheap items and the short term are inelastic.

points.title: Price elasticity of supply
points.brief: How much quantity supplied responds to a price change. Spare capacity, a short production period and goods that store well make supply more elastic.

points.title: Public goods
points.brief: Goods that are non-rival and non-excludable, such as street lighting, which markets under-supply because people can use them without paying.

points.title: Externalities
points.brief: Costs or benefits that fall on people outside a transaction. Negative ones, such as pollution, are over-produced; positive ones, such as education, under-produced.

points.title: Asymmetric information
points.brief: When one side of a deal knows more than the other, such as a used car seller, markets can give poor results.

points.title: Common access resources
points.brief: Resources that are rival but hard to exclude people from, such as fish stocks, which tend to be overused.

points.title: Government intervention to correct failure
points.brief: Indirect taxes, subsidies, regulation, advertising campaigns and direct provision can each correct a market failure.

points.title: Government failure
points.brief: An intervention can lower efficiency by accident, such as a rule that raises costs or a subsidy that keeps a wasteful industry going.

points.title: Material and non-material living standards
points.brief: Living standards depend on access to goods and services and on things such as the environment, health, safety and literacy.

points.title: The five-sector circular flow model
points.brief: Households, businesses, government, financial institutions and the overseas sector link through income, spending, saving, tax and trade.

points.title: The business cycle and its causes
points.brief: Shifts in aggregate demand and supply push the economy through expansion, peak, contraction and trough.

points.title: Aggregate demand factors
points.brief: Interest rates, consumer and business confidence, disposable income, the exchange rate and world growth change total spending.

points.title: Aggregate supply factors
points.brief: Productivity, the size and skills of the workforce, input costs, technology and natural events change the economy's capacity.

points.title: Strong and sustainable growth
points.brief: Growth in real GDP near the economy's long-run trend, about 3 per cent a year, that lifts living standards and can be kept up.

points.title: Growth that is too fast or too slow
points.brief: Growth that is too fast brings inflation, environmental harm and pressure on the current account. Growth that is too slow brings unemployment.

points.title: Full employment
points.brief: The lowest unemployment the economy can hold without inflation rising, called the natural rate (NAIRU), leaving only frictional and structural unemployment.

points.title: The labour force
points.brief: People are employed, unemployed, underemployed, hidden unemployed or long-term unemployed, and each tells a different story about jobs.

points.title: Measuring the labour market
points.brief: The unemployment rate, the participation rate and the labour force under-utilisation rate, which adds the underemployed to the unemployed.

points.title: Types of unemployment
points.brief: Cyclical unemployment comes from weak demand in a downturn. Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch of skills or places, and lasts longer.

points.title: The costs of unemployment
points.brief: High unemployment wastes output and tax revenue and harms people and communities. Unemployment that is too low can push up inflation.

points.title: Low and stable inflation
points.brief: The goal is inflation of 2 to 3 per cent on average. The CPI measures it, and underlying (core) inflation strips out prices that jump around.

points.title: Inflation, disinflation and deflation
points.brief: Inflation is rising prices, disinflation is prices rising more slowly, and deflation is prices falling.

points.title: Demand-pull and cost-push inflation
points.brief: Demand-pull inflation comes from spending growing faster than capacity. Cost-push inflation comes from rising costs of production.

points.title: Consequences of inflation
points.brief: High inflation erodes buying power, can start a wage-price spiral and distorts spending and investment. Inflation that is too low can delay spending and cost jobs.

points.title: Explaining recent results
points.brief: Changes in aggregate demand and supply explain how well Australia has met its growth, jobs and inflation goals over the past two years.

chapters.title: Trade and the balance of payments

points.title: Gains from trade
points.brief: Trade brings lower prices, more choice, access to resources, economies of scale, and more competition and efficiency.

points.title: The balance of payments
points.brief: A record of a country's transactions with the world. The current account covers trade and income; the capital and financial account covers investment.

points.title: The current account balance
points.brief: Australia usually runs a current account deficit. Cyclical influences such as commodity prices move it year to year; structural ones such as low saving keep it there.

points.title: Net foreign debt and equity
points.brief: Borrowing from overseas builds net foreign debt; selling shares and assets builds net foreign equity. Both come from funding investment with foreign saving.

chapters.title: The exchange rate, terms of trade and competitiveness

points.title: The exchange rate
points.brief: The price of the Australian dollar in another currency, set by demand and supply in the foreign exchange market.

points.title: Factors moving the exchange rate
points.brief: Interest rate gaps, commodity prices and the terms of trade, demand for exports and imports, foreign investment and inflation change demand for the Australian dollar.

points.title: The terms of trade
points.brief: An index of export prices over import prices. Commodity prices and costs in trading partners move it, and a rise means each export buys more imports.

points.title: International competitiveness
points.brief: How well Australian goods compete on price and quality overseas, shaped by productivity, costs, natural resources, the exchange rate and relative inflation.

points.title: Effects on the goals and living standards
points.brief: Changes in the exchange rate, the terms of trade and competitiveness shift exports, imports, jobs and inflation, and so the goals and living standards.

points.title: The Reserve Bank and its goals
points.brief: The RBA runs monetary policy under its charter, aiming for stable prices and full employment, independent of the government.

points.title: The cash rate
points.brief: The interest rate on overnight loans between banks. The RBA sets a target for it, and other interest rates follow.

points.title: Unconventional monetary policy
points.brief: When the cash rate is near zero, a central bank can buy bonds or lend cheaply to banks to push other interest rates down.

points.title: The transmission mechanism
points.brief: A change in the cash rate reaches spending through four channels: saving and investment, cash flow, the exchange rate, and asset prices and wealth.

points.title: The stance of monetary policy
points.brief: Policy is expansionary when rates are below neutral, contractionary when above, and neutral in between. Recent changes show which way the RBA leans.

points.title: Strengths and limits of monetary policy
points.brief: It can be changed quickly and is independent, but takes time to work fully and acts on the whole country at once.

points.title: The Commonwealth budget
points.brief: The government's yearly plan of revenue and spending. With monetary policy, it is used to steady aggregate demand over the business cycle.

points.title: Government revenue
points.brief: Direct taxes on income and indirect taxes on spending, which can be progressive, regressive or proportional, plus income from government businesses and asset sales.

points.title: Government spending
points.brief: Current spending on day-to-day services, capital spending on long-lasting assets, and transfer payments such as pensions.

points.title: Budget outcomes
points.brief: A balanced budget, a deficit or a surplus. The underlying cash balance, often shown as a share of GDP, is the usual measure.

points.title: Deficits, surpluses and public debt
points.brief: A deficit is funded by borrowing or selling assets and adds to public debt. A surplus can repay debt or be saved.

points.title: Automatic stabilisers
points.brief: Tax revenue and welfare spending move with the business cycle without any decision, softening booms and busts. This is the cyclical part of the budget.

points.title: Discretionary changes
points.brief: Deliberate changes to tax and spending, the structural part of the budget, such as cutting tax to lift spending in a downturn.

points.title: Expansionary and contractionary stance
points.brief: An expansionary budget adds to aggregate demand; a contractionary one takes from it. Recent budgets show which way policy leans.

points.title: Strengths and limits of budgetary policy
points.brief: It can target regions and groups, but it takes time to plan and pass, and debt has to be paid back.

points.title: Why supply-side policies matter
points.brief: Policies that improve the quantity and quality of resources, cut costs and lift productivity let the economy grow without inflation, alongside demand policies.

points.title: Education and training
points.brief: Spending on schools, universities and vocational training lifts workers' skills and productivity.

points.title: Research and development
points.brief: Grants and tax breaks for research encourage new products and methods that lift productivity.

points.title: Infrastructure
points.brief: Roads, rail, ports and digital networks cut business costs and raise the economy's capacity.

points.title: Tax reform
points.brief: Changes to the tax system that reward work, saving and investment, or cut the cost of doing business, can lift supply.

points.title: Skilled immigration
points.brief: Bringing in skilled workers adds to the population and workforce, fills skill gaps and can lift productivity and participation.

points.title: Trade liberalisation
points.brief: Cutting tariffs and other protection exposes firms to competition and cheaper inputs. It can cost jobs at first and lift efficiency later.

points.title: Market-based environmental policy
points.brief: Policies such as emissions trading put a price on pollution, changing costs now to protect resources for later generations.

points.title: Strengths and limits of supply-side policies
points.brief: They lift living standards in the long run, but take years to work and can be costly up front.
